widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def kfold_indices(n, k, seed):
    idx = np.arange(n)
    np.random.RandomState(seed).shuffle(idx)
    sizes = [n // k + (1 if f < n % k else 0) for f in range(k)]
    folds, start = [], 0
    for size in sizes:
        test = np.sort(idx[start:start + size])
        train = np.sort(np.concatenate([idx[:start], idx[start + size:]]))
        folds.append((train, test))
        start += size
    return folds

screens.title: The extreme: one loan at a time
screens.prose: More folds means bigger training sets. At $k = n$ each fold is a single loan: **leave-one-out** (LOO). The table shows four choices of $k$ on one dataset of 200 loans.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_score

def cv_mean_sd(X, y, k, seed):
    folds = KFold(n_splits=k, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
    scores = -cross_val_score(Ridge(alpha=1.0), X, y, cv=folds,
                              scoring='neg_mean_squared_error')
    return round(float(scores.mean()), 4), round(float(scores.std()), 4)

import numpy as np

def make_loans(n, p, seed):
    """Loans: spread over base rate (percentage points). x0 leverage +0.6, x1 interest cover -0.4,
    x2 sector risk +0.3, the rest pure noise; noise sd 0.45."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p)).round(3)
    beta = np.zeros(p)
    beta[:3] = [0.6, -0.4, 0.3][:p]
    y = (2.5 + X @ beta + rng.normal(0, 0.45, n)).round(3)
    return X, y

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def loo_mse(X, y):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    n = len(y)
    A = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), X])
    errors = []
    for i in range(n):
        keep = np.arange(n) != i
        coef = np.linalg.lstsq(A[keep], y[keep], rcond=None)[0]
        errors.append((A[i] @ coef - y[i]) ** 2)
    return round(float(np.mean(errors)), 4)

screens.title: What the number estimates
screens.prose: With fold MSEs $m_1, \dots, m_k$: $$\text{CV}_{(k)} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k} m_j.$$ Their sd is a rough guide to spread. It is not a standard error: $\text{sd}/\sqrt{k}$ assumes independent folds, but any two folds share most training rows. And no single model was tested: each fold had its own.
screens.question: What does the 5-fold estimate 0.1815 describe?

options.text: How well the recipe “fit ridge, $\alpha = 1$, on about 320 such loans” does on new loans
The error of the ridge model fitted on all 400 loans
options.why: That model was never tested; it did not exist during CV. The estimate is for the recipe that produced the five fold models.

options.text: The error of fold 3’s model, the worst one
options.why: Each fold’s model has its own score. The CV mean averages over five models.

feedback.correct: Cross-validation scores the procedure, not one fitted model.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which model was tested in each round.

explain.text: Five different models were fitted and tested, one per fold. Their average estimates what the fitting recipe achieves. The final model, fitted on all 400 loans, borrows that estimate, which is slightly pessimistic because it trains on more rows.

screens.title: MSE 0.21 ± 0.04
screens.prose: A credit model for loan spreads, in percentage points, is validated with 5 folds of 400 loans. The memo to the desk reads “CV MSE 0.21 ± 0.04”, where 0.04 is the sd of the five fold MSEs.
screens.question: What does the memo tell the desk?

options.text: A typical squared miss of 0.21, so a typical miss of about $\sqrt{0.21} = 0.46$ points; the five folds varied by about 0.04
The true MSE lies between 0.17 and 0.25 with 95% confidence
options.why: You read the fold sd as a confidence interval. Folds share training rows, so ± 0.04 is only a rough spread.

options.text: Predictions miss by 0.21 percentage points on average
options.why: You forgot the square. An MSE of 0.21 means a root mean squared miss of about 0.46 points.

options.text: Next year’s loans will score 0.21
options.why: The estimate is for new loans like these 400. A new year can differ; time is level 2’s subject.

hints.text: MSE is in squared units.
$\sqrt{0.21} \approx 0.46$.
The 0.04 is a spread across folds, not a standard error.

feedback.correct: About 46 basis points of typical miss, with fold-to-fold spread of 0.04.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take a square root, and remember what the 0.04 is.

explain.text: $\sqrt{0.21} = 0.458$, so a typical miss is about 46 basis points of spread. The ± 0.04 shows the folds roughly agree, nothing more. A desk would still lock a final test set, because CV numbers like this get used to choose models.

Shuffle exchangeable rows before cutting folds, stratify a rare class, and compare models on the same folds.
The CV mean estimates the fitting procedure’s error; the fold sd is a rough spread, not a standard error.
